claims.text: An active-learning-augmented machine-learning interatomic potential can reproduce solid and liquid free-energy surfaces for multicomponent high-entropy alloys and related binary systems.
The proposed potential can retain vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling effects.
The initial training data will consist of targeted high-temperature AIMD configurations from both solid and liquid states.
Active learning will add ab initio data in regions where model uncertainty is high.
Sampling rare configurations and states associated with strong electron–vibration coupling will improve coverage of critical regions.
The method is intended for temperatures from approximately 0.85 Tm to 1.15 Tm.
Validation will begin with elemental and binary prototypes before extension to alloys containing five or more components.
Mapping local atomic configurations to free-energy contributions ensures detailed representation of anharmonicity, vibrational entropy, and electron–vibration interactions.
Selective sampling combined with active learning can provide adequate coverage of the critical portions of the high-dimensional ab initio energy landscape.
Interpolation of the selectively sampled ab initio energy landscape will enable rapid free-energy estimates that closely match explicit AIMD results.
The proposed approach will reduce computational cost by approximately one order of magnitude relative to full ab initio molecular-dynamics methods.
Predicted phase free energies will match explicit AIMD benchmarks within a few meV per atom.
Performance outside the near-melting temperature range or stated compositional range is uncertain.
Reliable treatment of subtle electron–vibration coupling depends on active learning successfully sampling sparsely represented critical states.
Agreement in solid–liquid free-energy differences, melting entropy, and fusion volume change can test whether the ML potential reliably replaces full AIMD.

contradictions.description: The conditions specify 0.85–1.15 Tm, whereas the boundary describes the validated range as ±15–20% of Tm, which could extend to 0.80–1.20 Tm.
